translation: Perhaps because Miho and Satsuki see each other often in their hometown, they have similar expressions and manners of speaking.
Particularly, the way they eat sweets is the same—both use their manicured fingers to break a cookie into small pieces before bringing it to their mouths.
I try to remember if they always did this but my memory is vague.
The little habits and gestures I noticed when we last met might have simply faded away by now.
Miho is now married, having bought a second-hand house in her hometown where friends often gather.

Although there are times when she dreads going to her part-time job, it's her only connection to the world outside of the convenience store and a valuable opportunity to interact with "ordinary women in their thirties" like herself.
Therefore, she tries to accept Miho's invitations as much as possible.

Today too, with our group consisting of Miho, Yukari who brought along her young child, Satsuki who is also married but without any kids yet and myself; we gathered at Miho's home sharing cakes and tea.
At that moment, for the first time, I became a part of the world.
I felt as though I had been born anew.
As a functioning part of the world, I was certainly reborn that day.
For the two weeks leading up to the opening, we paired off and practiced tirelessly, serving imaginary customers or staff members.

We learned to make eye contact and smile, to bow politely, to bag feminine hygiene products separately from other items, to package hot and cold products separately and to sanitize our hands when handling fast food orders.

To familiarize us with handling cash, real money was kept in the registers during these drills though all receipts bore a large 'Training' stamp while our 'customers' were simply fellow part-timers dressed in uniform.
It felt rather like playing pretend shopping.
My sister, two years my junior, was a 'normal' child unlike me.
Yet she did not keep her distance, but rather adored me.
Whenever my sister would get scolded by our mother for some ordinary matter, I would approach our mother and ask, "Why are you angry?"
Once the scolding ended because of my question, my sister would always say "thank you" to me—perhaps thinking that I had shielded her from it.
Having little interest in sweets or toys myself, I often gave them to her instead.
As a result of this she was always following me around.
"Dad loves yakitori, let's cook and eat this today," I said.
When I repeated it in clear pronunciation, thinking she might not have heard me properly, my mother was taken aback.
The other neighbor's mother also widens her eyes and opens her mouth in surprise when hearing this.
I almost found it funny because of their funny faces, but when I noticed one of them staring at my hand, I realized that a single bird would not be enough.
"Should we get more?"
As looking over at several sparrows nearby walking side by side on the sidewalk, my startled mom finally came to her senses"Keiko!"
She shouted with a desperate voice as if reprimanding me.
"Sweetie! We need to give the little bird proper burial rites.
Look!
Others are mourning too; their friends have died and they must be lonely right?"
"Why? They're already dead.
Upon hearing my question Mother was left speechless.
I swiftly packed canned coffee, cigarettes, and an American hot dog into a small-sized bag.
During this time, the man who had been jingling coins in his pocket suddenly reached into his breast pocket as if he had just thought of something.
From that gesture, I quickly deduced that he was going to pay with electronic money.
"Welcome, good morning!"
Taking the canned coffee offered by a male customer with a light bow.
"Ah, and one of number 5 cigarettes.
" "Understood.
Quickly pulling out Marlboro Light Menthol and scanning it at the register.
"Please touch for age verification.
While the man touched the screen, I noticed his gaze swiftly shifted to the showcase filled with fast food and stopped my movements.
I could ask, "Would you like something else?", but when customers seem unsure about making a purchase, I prefer to step back and wait.
Reacting to the faint sound of loose change, I turn and look towards the register.
Many people who jingle coins in their hands or pockets are usually ones looking to quickly buy a newspaper or cigarette, so I'm highly attuned to the sound of money.
Sure enough, there is a man approaching the cash register with a canned coffee in one hand and his other hand plunged into his pocket.
I swiftly move inside of the store to slide behind  counter and stand ready so as not to keep customers waiting.
The convenience store is filled with sounds.
The chime of customers entering, the voice of an idol advertising new products over the store's radio.
The shout of staff, the sound of scanning barcodes.
The noise of items being placed in a basket, the sound of bread bags being grasped, and the echo of walking heels throughout the store.
All these sounds mix together to form "the sound of a convenience store," constantly resonating in my eardrums.
